questions.question: How do you remove duplicate values from an array in JavaScript?
questions.title: Remove duplicate array values in JavaScript
questions.direct_answer: For an array of primitive values, `const unique = [...new Set(values)]` removes duplicates and keeps the first occurrence order. Use a key-based Map when objects should be considered equal by an ID or another field.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: A Set stores each value once.
Spreading the Set creates a new array.
The first occurrence order is preserved.
Objects are compared by reference, not by matching fields.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
The simplest way to remove duplicate primitive values is to pass the array into a `Set` and convert the Set back to an array. A Set keeps one copy of each value and iterates in insertion order, so the first occurrence order remains visible.

For example, `[3, 1, 3, 2, 1]` becomes `[3, 1, 2]` with `[...new Set(values)]`. A manual loop with a Set is useful when the result also needs filtering or another calculation during the same pass.

This approach is usually O(n) average time and O(n) extra space. Two separate objects such as `{ id: 1 }` are different references, so a Set will keep both. To deduplicate objects by `id`, store them in a Map keyed by `id` and decide whether the first or last object should win.

sections.title: Set equality and object identity
sections.content:
Set uses JavaScript's SameValueZero equality. Values such as repeated strings, numbers, and the same object reference collapse to one entry. `NaN` also matches `NaN`, while `0` and `-0` are treated as the same value.

Object deduplication needs a business key. A Map can keep `id → object`; checking before insertion preserves the first record, while always calling `set` preserves the last record. That choice is part of the requirement, not a property of deduplication itself.

sections.title: Primitive and ID-based deduplication

questions.question: How do you find the first non-repeating character in a string?
questions.title: First non-repeating character with two passes
questions.direct_answer: Count every character in a Map, then scan the string again and return the first character whose count is one. The two-pass algorithm is O(n) time and O(k) space for k distinct characters.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: First pass builds character counts.
Second pass preserves the original order.
Return the first count of one.
Define case, spaces, and Unicode rules before coding.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
The reliable solution uses two passes. The first pass counts each character in a Map. The second pass follows the original string order and returns the first character whose count is exactly one.

For example, `swiss` has counts `s: 3`, `w: 1`, and `i: 1`. The second pass sees `s` first but skips it, then returns `w`. Trying to return while building counts can be wrong because a character that looks unique early may appear again later.

The algorithm is O(n) time and uses O(k) extra space for the distinct characters. The requirement should say whether `S` equals `s`, whether spaces count, and what to return when nothing is unique. A `for...of` loop reads Unicode code points more safely than indexing UTF-16 code units, although user-perceived symbols can still contain several code points.

sections.title: Frequency first, original order second
sections.content:
A frequency table answers how often each character appears, but a Map's key order alone should not replace the second scan. The required answer is based on the string's original position, so scanning the original sequence makes that rule explicit.

Text normalization changes the problem. A case-insensitive version can compare a normalized lowercase copy while returning the character from the original string. Full human-language comparison may also require Unicode normalization or grapheme-aware tools rather than a basic interview loop.

sections.title: Count, then locate

questions.question: How do you check whether two strings are anagrams in JavaScript?
questions.title: Anagram checking with character counts
questions.direct_answer: Normalize the two strings according to the requirement, reject unequal lengths, add counts for the first string, and subtract them for the second. Every final count must be zero for the strings to be anagrams.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Clarify case, spaces, and punctuation.
Unequal normalized lengths cannot be anagrams.
A frequency Map avoids relying on sort order.
Every character count must balance to zero.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Two strings are anagrams when they contain the same characters with the same frequencies, possibly after an agreed normalization. A frequency Map gives a linear scan: increment counts for the first string and decrement them for the second.

For example, after converting to lowercase, `listen` and `silent` have the same six letter counts. `hello` and `bello` fail when the second scan reaches `b`, because there is no available `b` count from the first word.

The count approach is O(n) average time and O(k) space. Sorting both strings is shorter in some interviews but normally costs O(n log n). Neither version can guess the text rules: ignoring spaces and punctuation, supporting accents, or comparing full grapheme clusters must be stated before normalization is added.

sections.title: Normalization and frequency balance
sections.content:
Length is a useful early check only after normalization. If the requirement ignores spaces, `rail safety` and `fairy tales` should have their spaces removed before their lengths and counts are compared.

A subtracting Map can fail early when a count is missing or already zero. Deleting keys whose count returns to zero is optional; it can make the final check as simple as `map.size === 0`, but it does not change the main complexity.

sections.title: Frequency-map anagram check

questions.question: How do you find the maximum sum of any subarray of size k?
questions.title: Fixed-size sliding window maximum sum
questions.direct_answer: Sum the first k values, then slide the window one position at a time by adding the incoming value and subtracting the outgoing value. This produces O(n) time instead of recalculating every window in O(nk).

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Build the first window once.
Add the incoming value.
Subtract the outgoing value.
Track the best sum after every move.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A fixed-size sliding window reuses the sum from the previous window. After calculating the first `k` elements, each move removes one value on the left and adds one value on the right.

For example, for `[2, 1, 5, 1, 3, 2]` with `k = 3`, the sums move from `8` to `7`, then `9`, then `6`. The maximum is `9`, produced by `[5, 1, 3]`. Only two arithmetic changes are needed per move.

The algorithm is O(n) time and O(1) extra space. It should reject `k <= 0` or `k > values.length`, and it must initialize the best value from the first window rather than from zero because every number may be negative.

sections.title: A rolling sum removes repeated work
sections.content:
The brute-force version adds the same middle values again for overlapping windows. The rolling sum keeps that shared work and changes only the two boundary values, which is the central sliding-window idea.

This exact method depends on a fixed window size. Variable-size problems, such as the shortest positive-number window reaching a target, move the left boundary according to a condition and need a different invariant.

sections.title: O(n) fixed window

questions.question: How do you rotate an array to the right by k positions?
questions.title: Rotate an array with normalized positions
questions.direct_answer: Normalize k with `((k % n) + n) % n`, then either join the last k values with the first n-k values or use the three-reversal method for an in-place rotation. Handle an empty array before taking a remainder by its length.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Reduce large k values with modulo.
Handle an empty array first.
Slice-and-join is simple but uses extra space.
Three reversals provide an in-place option.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A right rotation moves the last `k` values to the front while keeping their order. Because rotating by the array length changes nothing, `k` should first be normalized into the range from zero to `n - 1`.

For example, rotating `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]` right by `2` produces `[4, 5, 1, 2, 3]`. The clear non-mutating solution returns `values.slice(n - k).concat(values.slice(0, n - k))` after normalization.

That solution is O(n) time and O(n) extra space. If the requirement is truly in place, reverse the whole array, then reverse the first `k` values and the remaining values. The empty-array case must be handled before modulo, and the contract should say whether negative k means a left rotation.

sections.title: Modulo and the three-reversal invariant
sections.content:
Modulo removes complete rotations. The expression `((k % n) + n) % n` also turns a negative remainder into a valid positive offset when negative values are accepted.

The reversal method works because reversing the whole array places the two desired groups in front-to-back order but reverses each group internally. Reversing those groups restores their internal order while keeping the new group positions.

sections.title: Non-mutating right rotation
